utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, 31st of March, 2010. I would like to, first of all, greet the witness, the accused, including the people who are not here for various reasons, Defence counsel, all the members of the OTP, and more specifically Ms. West, who's going to conduct her cross-examination in a few minutes, and all the people assisting us. I believe the Registrar has an IC list of numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. 4D has submitted its response to the Prosecution's and other Defence objections to its documents tendered through Witness Milivoj Petkovic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01229. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber also wanted to indicate to Praljak's Defence that the Trial Chamber has deliberated on the request for certification to appeal. The Trial Chamber's decision will be filed either today or tomorrow. The Trial Chamber has deliberated on this issue, and based on that, it will not accept any request for reply whatsoever. Based on that, I wanted to ask Mr. Ibrisimovic whether he had any questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ibrisimovic. Ms. West, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic. My name is Kim West; I'm with the Office of the Prosecution. I'm going to be asking you some questions this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, yesterday you told the Trial Chamber that your promotion in November of 1993 had been proposed by Mr. Coric, and we saw a document in regard to that. Were you ever actually promoted?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not promoted. The document that we saw yesterday was only a proposal, and it coincided, more or less, with the departure of Mr. Coric to a position in the civilian police. And since at that time I was, pursuant to his permission, sent to Zagreb for professional additional training at the Faculty of Criminology in Zagreb, where I and one of my colleagues from the service attended subjects dealing with crime tactics and methods and technology and techniques, so very soon after that I went to Zagreb for this professional training. And there was some personnel changes within the entire Military Police Administration, so that the proposal never took effect as it was set out; not only regarding myself, but many of the other people from the list as well. So, in actual fact, after that I did not go back to the Crime Investigation Department of the Military Police in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you actually left the military police in December of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So up until the time of the proposal, up until November of 1993, where was your office?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until my departure to Ljubuski, I worked throughout in the offices in Mostar, in Mostar Centre; first of all, in the building of the medical school, which at the beginning of the war was right up at the front-line, and then afterwards in the Mechanical Engineering Faculty building, on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you a map, and this is going to come up on your screen, and we're going to turn to Sanction. The map is P11236. And I think -- sir, can you see that now? Not yet. This is a map that the Trial Chamber is familiar -- I think everyone's familiar with it. We've seen it before. But this is the map that the Trial Chamber used on its tour of the region. It's 11236. Mr. Vidovic, let's focus specifically on May of 1993. Where was your office?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the office I worked in was in the Machine Engineering Faculty building. Do you want me to point it out to you or --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. And would that be number 14 on this map? Is that a good representation of the location?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbers are very small here. I can barely see them. Where it says "Strelcevina," [phoen] above that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell me if that's number 14?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so number -- do you see the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is that number 16, that's just above number 14?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you see the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is that number 13, that appears to be a bit below number -- the Mechanical Faculty building?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that those locations, the stadium and the Vranica building were close to your office?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not far. Vranica, and then some 250 to 300 metres, and the stadium at 100 metres distance from the building I worked in.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, could you -- I'm not sure if the Trial Chamber prefer that he sign the hard copy or if he signs on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No signature needed, because he did not write anything on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Although he has now testified in regard to the map, it would be my position that that would be enough to authenticate the map. But I can have him also write on it as well, if that would be satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, why don't you sign it, and we'll give it an exhibit number, since we know that you have located the stadium, the office, and the Vranica building, 13, 14 and 16. Sign it, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be given Exhibit IC01230. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A little correction. The numbers are really not easy to read. It's 15 and not 16. 13, 14, and 15 are the identified numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to talk a little bit about your testimony yesterday, and specifically Judge Antonetti asked you a question -- excuse me. This is from Monday. It's from the daily transcript, 29, but you'll see it on the screen. And this is what he said: "What I would like to know is this: Please listen carefully. When a report is drafted for it to be sent on to the military prosecutor, do you always ask for permission from the military unit commander whom the soldiers belong to, or don't you ask him anything whatsoever, you simply forward the report to the military prosecutor?" And your answer was this: "We were autonomous in all matters with regard to the criminal reports. We were a sort of a service of the public -- of the Military Prosecutor's office, and all our criminal reports went to them. We never applied to any military commander to allow us to submit our criminal reports to the military prosecutor." So, Mr. Vidovic, is it fair to say that your decisions to investigate cases were not based off of the interests of other members of the HVO? Those decisions that you made, they were independent and autonomous; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And those decisions were not at all influenced by the identity of the alleged perpetrator, whether that person be Muslim, Serbian, or Croatian; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And nor were those decisions influenced by the identity of the victims? For example, if the victims were non-Croats, that didn't sway your decision not to investigate; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, many of the people arrested on the 30th of June and the days thereafter were taken to the Heliodrom; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you became involved in that process; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you describe for us your involvement?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this: I and the service that I worked for never took part in taking people away to Heliodrom. We were involved in writing down and registering them. And they were disarmed members of the HVO of Muslim ethnicity, and what we did was -- under orders from the operative zone, for a few days we would take down basic information about them; their names, and surnames, and the units they belonged to. So let me repeat. We did not participate, I and my service, in any taking of people to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And we're just going to focus right now about -- in regard to that registration. Those people that you registered in early July and late June, those people were Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our department started this registration about three or four days after the conflict broke out; that is to say, after the attack by the BH Army on North Camp. And so most of the people registered were members of the HVO of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And those people who were brought to the Heliodrom, those Muslim men, were brought there to ensure that they wouldn't then fight for the ABiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were disarmed, following orders from the unit commander in which they had taken part, and they are disarmed for security reasons, precisely the way you put it, so as not to commit treason within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it was the fact that they were Muslims that formed their grounds of allegiance to the ABiH; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the 30th of June was the day when the BH Army attacked the Croatian Defence Council around North Camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, yesterday you spoke about this earlier in the day, and you, for the most part, reiterated what you just said. On page 9 of the daily transcript, you said that you were there to make a list of all the detainees who were then disarmed by the HVO -- of the HVO, who were Muslim, and whose units had isolated them and put them at Heliodrom. You also said that you made a list, and you said you had the basic details of the person there; the names, the surname, where they were from. You said it was just the basics. You said that those lists were handed over to the warden of the prison. And when asked by Judge Antonetti about who was in a position to free those people, your answer was: "I didn't know under whose authority they were or who had the authority to do that." And a further question from the President as regards to the status of those people who were there, you said that: "The ones that I interviewed and whose details I took down, they were HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, in the vast majority of cases." Sir, we're going to focus on that, and we're going to look at what Josef Praljak said about the those interviews and look at his testimony. Excuse me, Josip Praljak. He testified in front of the Trial Chamber about this very issue, and this is going to be on Sanction. And this is from February 26, 2007. Thank you. And, sir, when asked about the Muslim men who were brought to the Heliodrom in the first part of July - you'll see this on the screen, you'll have it translated - he said: "We never established the number of people who arrived, because that job, the job of taking them in and registering them, registering those who were arriving, was done by 10 to 12 employees of the MUP, of the military police, of the SIS, with Zvonko Vidovic at its head." Sir, would you agree with me that that testimony was correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't at the head of any group. All I did was work at the head of my department. As I've already said, Josip Marcinko was my superior, and from orders -- on orders from Marcinko, with the same MUP employees and employees of the military police and SIS, were sent there simply to do my job, to do the work with regard to registering and listing. So I don't know where he gets this from, the fact that I was its head.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, we're going to move to the next part of the transcript for Mr. Praljak, and it's just a little bit later, in which he speaks a little bit more about this. And the question was: "Can you tell the Judges more what was said or understood by you as to the role of Mr. Zvonko Vidovic in doing the intake or reception of these people who were coming to the Heliodrom prison ..." The answer was: "... Vidovic informed Bozic, and I was present, that all the registration and taking over of the people who had arrived would be carried out by his people and that they would compile a complete list of the people brought in, which list would be handed over to the prison." Sir, do you agree with that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll repeat what I said a moment ago. I took part with those same people from the MUP, SIS, the military police, the Crime Department, in compiling the registration, and all the lists we made, we handed over to Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going -- thank you. I'm going to show you a list of names now. They're on the screen, and I'm going to ask if you recognise any of these names. Were these people with whom you worked during registration at the Heliodrom? Do you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There are four names in front of you. Do you recognise all four?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's just a mistake here. The first two names, there's a spelling mistake. It's Stjepan Rubinic and Toni Ramljak with a J, R-a-m-l-j-a-k. But otherwise, yes, those are people who worked with me in the department, the Crime Investigation Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Ms. West, how will this get into the record? It is -- we see four names on the screen, and that is absolutely all that we see.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. I think perhaps the best way is to mark this for identification or perhaps I can have the witness himself just testify to the names. I did this only for my own aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But could you perhaps say where it comes from? Because there, it comes from the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think further on in the cross-examination, we'll discover that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, these four people, can you tell us what their names were. And putting aside my spelling mistakes, can you tell us the four people with whom you worked.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation is a little strange, but I get the gist of it. Let me repeat, they were people who worked with me in the same Department for Crime Prevention.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And tell us the names of those four people, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1, Toni Ramljak, l-j, number 2, Stjepan Rubinic, with an R. Number 3, Zeljko Kovic; and number 4, Damir Cipra.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, now we're going to turn to the binders, which I believe you probably have there, and there's a total of three binders. And my hope is most of these exhibits are grouped according to subject matter so that we can move fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a while ago you said that the interpretation sounded strange to you. What did you mean, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lady doing the interpretation stopped a bit, paused, so I couldn't follow the gist of the whole interpretation, but ultimately she told me what she meant. So first I didn't quite understand because she was a little hesitant, so that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you have binder 1 in front of you, and it's separated into parts. And we're going to go to part 4, which is the last part at the back. And perhaps in the beginning the witness could have the usher's assistance. We're going to part 4. There we go, thank you. And specifically we're going to go to Exhibit P0304.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, I'm looking at the list of documents. Have all the documents been admitted or have some not been admitted yet? In order to avoid the discussion on probative value and relevance, it would be desirable, if a document has not been admitted, to let us know that it has not already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you, Mr. President, I'll do so. P03040 is an admitted document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this is a list of persons taken to the Central Military Remand facility, 30 June 1993. It's a total of 124 persons. It's signed by Stefan Rubinic, one of the individuals you just mentioned. Is this a list that's familiar to you? Have you seen this type of list before?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this specific list before. But, roughly speaking, they're the types of lists that we're talking about. I haven't seen this one, in particular, because Stjepan Rubinic was doing that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we look at number 1, we have a name, we have a date of birth, we have an address, and we have what I'll term a job, "member of the HVO." If we look at number 2, we've got a name, a date of birth, an address, and then again what looks to be a job, and then a status. He says he's unemployed. And if we took some time and we went through all 124 names, I can tell you, Mr. Vidovic, we would see the same -- we'd see the same thing; the name, the address, the date of birth, and then what their status was, whether they had a job, whether they're in the HVO, or whether they have a civilian job, or whether they're unemployed or a pensioner. Sir, now, if this is the type of list that was created when you did your registration, you would agree with me that when you told the Trial Chamber that you took down just the basics, the basics would include the person's job or their status?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And of this list, this example of one of the lists that was taken, there's 124 people. And just let me tell you, for the purposes of this question, I looked through the entire list, and I determined from the information that was written down that there were 29 HVO members and there were 95 civilians or people who were employed in a job that was not the military. And there was also 12 pensioners listed, people over the age of 50. So, Mr. Vidovic, my question for you is: Of this list, where about 23 per cent of the entire list were HVO members and 77 per cent of the entire list were civilians, would you agree that that general percentage represents the people that you met on June 30th and registered in the days afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say to this question is this: I've already said that under orders, we were engaged to make these lists. I, nor my people from the department, brought those people to the Heliodrom in the first place. Now, the military units who disarmed them probably had a reason for doing so. That's one point. The second point is this --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me. So I think we're going to probably have this problem in the hours to come, but I asked you whether this list, in a general way, represented the number of civilians and HVO members that were registered on those days, and your answer is not responsive to my question. So we're going to try it again. I would ask that you focus on my question and try to give an answer that's responsive. In this list in front of you, there are 124 people. Twenty-three per cent of those people are HVO members, Muslim HVO members, but 77 per cent are civilians. Would you agree with me that when you did the registration at Heliodrom, and when you testified before this Chamber that for the most part those people were HVO members, that you were incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat once more that at the moment when we were making those lists, we had no way of verifying what these people had said to us, like that they had been drafted or not, so we took whatever they said for granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Then that's a different issue. Sir, are you now telling the Trial Chamber when they told you they were an HVO member, you had no way of verifying that, but nonetheless you put it down on the list, didn't you? And when I say "you," I mean you and the people with whom you worked.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So when these people told you that they worked at Soko Aircraft Industry and they were now unemployed, you put that down on a list, but you just didn't verify it; is that what you're telling us now?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we were to look at all the lists from Heliodrom that were created from the beginning of July, those lists would include information about the status of the registry; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that you gave those lists to the prison, but I'd like to look at Mr. Praljak's diary in regard to what he said about the list. And this is P00352. It's in the same section of that binder. It's binder 1, part 4, and it's P00352.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 352. Do you see that? Thank you. And this is an admitted exhibit, and the Trial Chamber has seen it before, and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm not going to bore Ms. West by -- or bother her by interrupting her, but I have two questions. I'm looking at the list because I'm interested in the members. I see, for instance, that there is a person there; it's number 73. And the son of this person works for the military police. So the son works for the military police, and we arrest the father. Look at number 86 now. This person seems to have an immunity certificate which has been signed by Zeljko Siljeg or somebody else; I don't know. It is rather strange, isn't it? How do you explain that those people have been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can only go back to what I've already said, that we saw those people for the first time at the Heliodrom. So I cannot provide a good explanation how a person was taken in, whose son was in the military police. I said yesterday that members of the military police at that time did not disarm their fellow soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, at least as far as our battalion in Mostar is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My apologies, Ms. West. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at P00352. This is the diary, and specifically we're going to go to page 28 of the English. But I'm looking for the July 9th entry, and I think that will help you. The July 9th entry indicates -- sir, you may have that in front of you on the screen. It indicates that Praljak wrote down: "I asked Zvonko to send me a list of prisoners. He said I would get it as soon as it was completed." And then if we go to July 30th, which is the same page of the English, it's the next entry, there is a meeting with the warden, and he writes down: "I asked Zvonko Vidovic to finally send a list of the prisoners, and he always says, 'You will get it.'" Mr. Vidovic, is it possible that, at least by July 30th, you had not yet sent a list to the prison?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these are our lists, the lists of the Crime Department and of the register of persons who we are processing in our criminal investigations, because at the time we already had the problem with the people on who are worked and the problem of these disarmed people who were put up in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vidovic. Well, let's look at what Mr. Pusic said about this subject matter. We're going to go to P04141. It's the same section of the binder, P04141. This is an admitted exhibit, and this is from August 9th. This is a decision, and under number 1 he writes: "All detainees will be registered using a personal data slip filled in by themselves and checked by the prison warden, who is charged with completing a list of detainees and supplying it, as well as the proposed personal data slips, to this commission. For the purpose of classification, it is desirable that along with the name of the detainee, all the directives are known to the prison warden shall be entered with regard to the proper practice of physically accommodating them separately (BH Army prisoners by location of capture, et cetera)." So, sir, would you agree with me that at least by August 12th at the Heliodrom, there's still a problem with classification of the prisoners; in other words, they don't know who's an HVO Muslim detainee, and they don't know who's a civilian, and they don't know who's a BH Army prisoner, and they still have not physically separated them? Would you agree with me that that's the case?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And also in a very general way, and this is a general question, would you agree that the inability to separate the prisoners by status might cause difficulties for the prison?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the prison, at any rate, yes. It was a big problem for my service, too. I have lists of persons with whom I work in my service, but -- or I had at the time, but I was already faced with the situation that the people on who I worked, in the framework of criminal investigations, are mixed up with these others, they're not separated. And that's not only a problem of the prison, but also of our department.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So then let's first talk about the problem for the prison. Would one of the problems for the prison be this: that when HVO unit commanders came in and wanted to take the prisoners out for labour, there was no way for the prison to determine the status of the people who were going out for labour? Would that be one of the problems?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And let's go back to the diary. It's P0352, P00352. And we're going to go to the next page in the English, which is page 29. Specifically, it's the entry for September 22nd, 1993. And in this entry, Mr. Praljak writes that he had spoken to Stanko Bozic, and he writes: "Army members and civilians have not yet been separated to avoid releasing wrong people, to prevent an army soldier leaving instead of a civilian. Some are said to have left in this way." Now, Mr. Praljak is talking about a different problem than I was talking about, but would you agree with me that, nonetheless, by September 22nd there is still no classification and segregation of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly what happened in late September. I can tell where I was at the time, but I cannot reply with a yes or no to your question because I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fair enough. Sir, we're going to go to P0341 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Witness. My apologies for taking the floor. But on numerous occasions, and even yesterday you said that people who were arrested were disarmed, and you repeat this again and again. So I can easily understand that for security reasons, you have to disarm people. But when looking closely at the list, I see that number 50 and number 120 are doing humanitarian work, which would mean that people doing humanitarian work are armed to the teeth. But I also note that number 9, who is of Muslim ethnicity, has a wife who is Croat. So we are arresting someone, and the wife of this person is Croat. So we are arresting people doing humanitarian work that are supposedly armed, as well as people of mixed ethnicity. So how do you explain this? Do you continue to say that all those people were armed and that they were disarmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat once more, Your Honour, that we came to the Heliodrom and only there did we receive information about those people. All these are things that I heard, and not saw. That's what I want to stress. We met them for the first time when we started registering them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were told that those people were disarmed, and so you're telling me you that you heard about it, but you had no idea, yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P03411. It's in the same part of that binder, P03411.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is remarks and instructions authored by you, and it's 12 July 1993. And I think you testified about this yesterday. You indicated it was to -- well, it says it's to the Military Remand Prison. Let's just look at a little bit of your testimony from yesterday. It's going to come up on Sanction. It's J, and I apologise to the usher for this back and forth, but I can just read this. This is your testimony from March 30th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI SAID
utterances.text: "Well, who was in a position to free those people?" And you said: "At that time, I didn't know under whose authority they were or who had the authority to do that." So I'd like to look at this document, 3411. And under number 1, you wrote: "Until further notice, it is forbidden to release any detainees using the procedure and practice of the recent days. Any possible exceptions must be requested from and approved by the chief of the Military Police Administration, Mr. Valentin Coric, or his deputy, Mr. Lavric, and it will be pointed out that they are exceptions." So this is what you wrote almost two weeks after the prisoners started coming into the Heliodrom. So, sir, would you agree with me that the only person who has the ability to release any of those detainees, according to what you wrote, is Mr. Coric or Mr. Lavric?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. This letter refers exclusively to the persons under the jurisdiction of our Crime Department, who we were processing. We worked on them every day, and Stanko Bozic and Mr. Praljak know them as persons from the Crime Department. So this, what we're looking at, only refers to persons under our jurisdiction. In those days, it was known to happen that they would take people with whom we were working.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So under number 3, it says: "Visits to the detainees are not allowed, or the delivery of any food, messages, and the like, except with the written approval of the chief of the Mostar Section," and that being you. So does this regard only those people upon whom you were investigating; is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so to the extent of that group of people -- to the extent that you were involved with that group of people, what percentage of them were at the Heliodrom? Excuse me, strike that. What percentage of the total population at the Heliodrom comprised that group of people?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the people we were investigating?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here and now, after almost 17 years, I cannot really go into percentages, but I can say that it was a substantial number of persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So would you say it's the majority of the people there? Is it more than 50 per cent of the people there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't wish to speculate about percentages. I simply cannot say, here and now, after almost 17 years. But I can say that it was large number because all members of our section had a relatively large number of cases that they were investigating or they were about to file criminal reports against, because we were faced with a large number of criminal offences daily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question of a technical nature. I see that the way you work is almost similar to the one in my country, but I would like to have some clarification on one issue. When a policeman is interviewing a witness, is he in a position to free this person or does this policeman have to obtain the agreement of the prosecutor for the rest of the procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in our work there were two aspects of what you are talking about, so there was police detention up to 12 hours and police detention of up to 72 hours with a permission issued by the investigating judge. In the latter case, we would have to inform the investigating judge of the existence or non-existence of grounds for additional detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So another technical question. Amongst those that were at the Heliodrom, did you check those that were detained for 12 hours already and those who after three days had to be referred to the discretion of an investigating judge, or did you not take this into account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the ones we were registering, the disarmed members?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our registering work was completed, as far as our department was concerned. We had nothing more to do with them after we had registered them and handed over the lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, to the extent that there was a substantial number of these types of detainees, do you concede, then, that the military police was responsible at least for them?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend, but it seems that the question is unclear. Perhaps you could make yourself clear who exactly you're referring to, the ones from the lists or the ones being investigated for criminal offences, because there was an interruption so the witness may not actually know which group you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the ones who were investigated, the ones that you were just speaking about with Judge Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you then repeat the entire question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Those individuals who you were talking about, the ones who were under investigation, the substantial number who remained at the Heliodrom, do you concede that the military police was responsible for them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as our Crime Department was concerned, where I worked too, we only did work from our remit. They were put up at the Heliodrom, and the people working at the Heliodrom were supposed to take care of all other aspects of their stay there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to go to P05477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, I do not find this question very satisfactory. There are two things. One is the question whether a person is detained and someone has the responsibility for the fact that a person is deprived of his or her liberty. Another matter is the specific execution of detention; at what time they get breakfast, when they can see a doctor, where they sleep, and so forth. Am I correct that when you said this was a matter of Heliodrom, you referred to the second aspect; namely, the practical execution of the deprivation of liberty, whereas you have not answered the question who is responsible for the decision whether they are or not deprived of their liberty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll repeat what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please do not repeat. I put a question, and try to answer this question. You don't have to repeat, because I've heard what you've said. And if that had been satisfactory, I would not have put the question. Can you make -- can you tell me whether the military police was responsible for the fact of deprivation of liberty? Not how it was carried out in practice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police was not responsible for the deprivation of liberty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And it was also, as you said, not responsible for how the people were held, because that was Heliodrom, and the result is that you say the military police was in no way responsible for this class of detainees; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean the Crime Department of the Military Police, where I worked, then, yes, we were not responsible for detaining or depriving of liberty the HVO detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that clarifies your answer. Excuse me, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I have to correct the transcript. On page 25, line 16, the witness said "the HVO soldiers," not "HVO detainees." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 5477. This is the same binder, but it's part 2 of the binder. So it's towards the front, part 2, P05477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have that in part 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Then that's my mistake, and as long as you have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you have that, sir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a September 29th letter to Mr. Stojic, and it's from you. And in the very -- well, counsel for Mr. Petkovic asked you about this document yesterday, and she focused, I believe, on a certain part of it. But I'm going to look at another part of it. In the beginning, the very first paragraph, you are talking about an incident that has damaged the development of the situation in the military and civilian HR-HB HVO, and in the second paragraph you talk specifically about this problem. And you wrote: "Last week, during the most fierce military operations in the Mostar region, HVO soldiers came to Heliodrom, which is currently being used as a detention centre for civilians, with a note that said that the bearer should be allowed to take away the prisoners of his choosing. Among those chosen, all of whom were Croats housed in the remand centre, were four murderers," and you list the names: "And the last one was detained as a civilian and will therefore face a civil court, also for the crime of murder."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I don't know whether the problem is that the interpreter doesn't have the document before her or whether Ms. West is speaking too fast, but the witness is getting just every fifth word of the document. So perhaps he could be allowed to read it for himself in Croatian, because otherwise, just listening to the interpretation, he can't understand what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you can take a moment and read that second paragraph. That describes the problem you were complaining about. And under the third paragraph, you say that: "The above-mentioned note was signed by Mr. Tuta ..." So, Mr. Vidovic, you indicated that the Heliodrom was currently being used as a detention centre for civilians. When you wrote that, were you talking about the civilians who had been arrested after June 30th?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I don't know whether the problem lies in the reading of the text or whether it's the interpretation, but it says "which is at the moment being used as a detention facility for civilians." "Detention," is the word used, "for civilians," and not as a detention centre. As a remand prison, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, I'll take either one, "detention facility" or "detention centre for civilians."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you wrote --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. West, but you should take it as remand prison, not detention centre. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, go to the -- you have the Croatian version in front of you. I want you to read out paragraph 2. And as you read it, it will be translated for the Court. You can read it out loud. Sir, read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this, that starts "Naime"? "Last week, during the fiercest military operations in the Mostar region in the premises of the Central Military Remand Prison of Heliodrom, which is currently being used as a detention centre for civilians ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, that's enough. Thank you. So when --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but -- [Interpretation] I apologise, but that's not the right translation. "Pritvor" is not translated as "detention centre," but as "remand prison." I would really ask the interpreters to be precise, because this is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another important thing that the witness said which wasn't interpreted. He said "and as 'pritvor.'" The "i" or "and" is being left out, because this way it turns out that it is just as "pritvor." And I see that in the English version of the document, this "and" is missing, which in this case would be "and" or "also." The "i," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness says, I did say "i," meaning "and."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, this debate will be decided by the Trial Chamber. What I want to focus on is the word "civilians." When you wrote that, what type of people were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll finally answer. It's like this: What I'm writing here on the date stipulated above exclusively refers to the latter part of the text. And in the latter part of the text, it is very clear what I want to say. Gentlemen Bijuk, Anic, and Drmac, they were people who were permanent clients, if I can put it that way, of our department, and at this point in time, well, I say that they're murderers, that they had committed the crime of murder. And this detention for civilians, well, Madam Prosecutor, you see that Drago Klemo was detained as a civilian. So if you followed carefully what I said earlier on about the civilian prison in Santiceva Street, which was called Celovina, that at the beginning of the conflict, when it broke out, because of the front-line, he was transferred to Heliodrom and then was used -- which was then used as a civilian -- for civilian detention. So apart from Drago Klemo, on the premises of Heliodrom there were other civilian suspects, that is to say, people suspected of having committed various crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, the crux of this letter is your complaint, and this complaint is addressed to Stojic. So if we go to page 3 of the English, and this is where you list a number of points, and it starts with: "I would hereby like to ask you the following," Stojic, "the following: "To agree at the highest level on a united position with regard to HVO units not interfering in military or civilian police affairs ..." And then you list something else. And the third thing is what Ms. Alaburic focused on. But if we go to the fourth point, you say: "With all due respect to combat readiness and morale of the HVO soldiers, I would hereby also like to ask you to explain to certain commanders once more that they should not count on detainees who are under investigation until their case is finished ..." Sir, you sent this letter to Mr. Stojic to complain about Tuta. Did you get a response from Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: In my work at this time, I began to encounter this problem more and more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse, Mr. Vidovic, and I apologise for interrupting. But the question I asked you calls for a yes-or-no answer. And then we can talk about it a little bit more, but my question is: Did you get a response from Mr. Stojic, whether verbal or written?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, why did you address it to Mr. Stojic? Did you think he was in a position to do something about Tuta?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for that reason, because apart from writing to Mr. Stojic, I also was writing to the military commanders. There were several addressees, so I was trying to find ways and means of coming to grips with the situation. Somebody had to decide. So here I'm just informing various officials about what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to Mr. Stojic, you also put on notice other HVO military commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that was because you felt they were in a position to do something to control Tuta?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to go to P03133. This is, I think, the same part 4 of that binder. P03133. This is an admitted exhibit as well. This is July 3rd, and again it's a special report signed by you. And if we can go to the fourth paragraph. It's the same subject matter we were just talking about. You say: "This department objects to poor security for the detained persons provided by the 1st Military Police Battalion." And then you say: "For example, at 1900 hours on July 2nd," I think that should be 1993, "an unknown soldier (supposedly from the 2nd Brigade, 3rd Battalion) entered the hall where Muslims were and lined up 12 persons with the intentions of taking them away, without anyone's authorisation. I personally prevented him, even though the building was secured by three military policemen. Please ask the security commander to reinforce security measures. Combat activities are carried out inside the barracks, and prisoners should not walk around freely without written authorisation." So you say that an unknown soldier entered the hall where Muslims were lined up, and there were 12 persons, with the intention of taking them away. Sir, do you have any idea whether those Muslims -- or what the status were of those Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably those disarmed members of the HVO who were Muslims by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you say "probably." Why do you say "probably"? What makes you think they were disarmed HVO Muslim members? Did they have different clothes that suggested that? Were they segregated in a room, where you knew there were only Muslim detainee HVO soldiers? How did you know they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers with whom I had daily contacts with when I was given an assignment, they were exclusively in the Heliodrom building. The people I worked with were exclusively in Heliodrom, or, rather, detained in Heliodrom. And that's why I said "probably," because actually I had no contact with them. They were just people who were in Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to go back to Sanction, and we're going to look at some more testimony from Mr. Praljak. And this was the cross-examination of Mr. Praljak by Ms. Alaburic, and she was talking about where these people were located and what their status was. And she says: "All right. Now, what about the HVO soldiers who were brought to the Heliodrom? Regardless of their ethnicity, what status did they have?" The answer was: "During that period of time, and they were brought into the prison, we didn't know they were the Muslims or whether they were the HVO units or not. "Q. Are you telling us, then, Mr. Praljak, and can you confirm that in the facilities that you mentioned, that is to say, the prison, the school, and the sports hall, that there were both HVO soldiers there who were Muslims and soldiers of the BH Army, and perhaps some third category?" And his answer was, "Yes." And if we can just skip to the bottom, the question is: "Mr. Praljak, when you received requests and demands to release prisoners to perform labour or detainees to perform labour, did you need to contact the administration of the detention centre? Did the administration of the detention centre have to see about this?" And the answer was: "When the order to release these people came, the shift commander did not differentiate between persons. He did not differentiate the different categories, but they would take these persons from prison out in set order." Mr. Vidovic, you earlier this morning indicated the lack of -- sorry. You earlier indicated that the lack --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. The witness has not received the interpretation. You're going too fast, and the interpreter can't follow. And this is a specific question which refers to people being released for labour, to perform labour, to release prisoners to perform labour. All the witness heard through the interpretation was "release," not "released to perform labour," so I think we should go slower and so that every word can be translated, because it's not the same to release someone or to release them to perform labour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, we are talking about the issue of release for labour. And would you agree with me that part of this -- let's call it a disorganisation. Part of the problem was without a system of classification, without a system of segregation, whether it be purposeful or not, then prisoners could be taken out without any understanding as to whether they were civilians, whether they were ABiH prisoners of war, or whether they were HVO Muslim detainees; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether you're right or not, because I didn't take part in what the commanders of the military units did with the release of their detained armed members -- disarmed members.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P06170. It's part 4 of binder 1, same part, P06170. This is October 27th, and it's a report on the work of the Detainee Release Commission. And this is a --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 6170. It's in part 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct. This is October 27th, 1993, and there was testimony from Mr. Praljak about his. He indicated that it was delivered to Mr. Stojic. And I'm not going to go through the whole letter, but if we go the -- excuse me, to the penultimate paragraph, so towards the end, it says: "I must mention that the SIS and the Crime Investigative Service have still not segregated the Muslim armed force members from the others. And simply segregating them in another building would prevent such events because the release of detainees would be open to inspection." Mr. Vidovic, I'm only focused on this issue of segregation. Would you agree with me that even by October 27th, segregation had still not happened at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just take a moment to read through this, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you now repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: By October -- would you agree with me that by October 27th, segregation had still not happened at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. At the end of October? Well, I was already leaving the Crime Mostar Centre in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We haven't left yet, so we're going to go to November. We're going to go to P06729. It's the same part, P06729. This is a report -- a SIS report -- a Military Police Sector report in relation to the work of the prisoners at Gabela and Heliodrom. I'm going to English page 5, and it's the heading "The Accommodation of Prisoners of War." There you go. It's the heading "The Accommodation of Prisoners of War." And it says: "In said facilities," we're talking about Gabela and the Heliodrom, "there are 2,600 prisoners of war who are of the same category as prisoners of war in the previous shelter of the same category; i.e., real prisoners of war have not been separated." And then there's a dash, and it says: "Members of the BH Army have not been separated from civilians who've been brought 'for various reasons.'" Mr. Vidovic, November 18th, would you agree that at the Heliodrom the civilians have still not been separated from, in this case, BH Army prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that, because we're dealing with the 18th of November here, and at the time, based on my calculations, I had already ceased to be an employee of the Crime Department. And if you remember the 11th of November and the proposal for an appointment, I was in Ljubuski from the end of October, and I don't think I was in the police at this time. I think I was in Zagreb already. So I don't know what was happening at Heliodrom, and I've never been to Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, you're saying November 18th, you're not involved in any of this anymore?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would be right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to part 2 of that binder, so if you back up and go to part 2 of that binder, P06702. P06702, I hope I'm correct, in part 2. This is a November 17th letter, so the day before, from you, in which you sign it: "Chief of the Military Police Crime Investigation Department." And you say: "On November 10th, 1993, we were informed by the Military Court about the illegal release of a remand prisoner, Kozul ..." And then you say: "In talks with the chief, Mr. Coric, we learned that Kozul ... was released ..." And it goes on. And my point is, sir, on the November 17th, you are still well involved with what's going on in the military police, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Ljubuski, precisely. I got the dates mixed up, but I was in Ljubuski at the time, as acting head of the Crime Department, but I left very soon after that. By the end of November, I wasn't in the military police anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you mention your talks with Mr. Coric. Sir, how often did you talk with Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were working in Mostar, very rarely, hardly at all. And when we came to Ljubuski, we met there for a few days, because, as I said, he was leaving, going to the Ministry of the Interior, and I was leaving for Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But during the time when you were in Mostar, if a big event happened or an incident of note happened, on those occasions would you talk to Mr. Coric about those events?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't able to talk to Mr. Coric. I wasn't in a position to do that because we worked in a department which, in hierarchical terms -- well, as regards some letters by Mr. Coric to our department, in most cases they had to do with recommendations for work, because the Military Police Administration, which was in Ljubuski, was a sort of, well, let's say, administrative centre, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What about those occasions, sir, when you were in Mostar, when you were notified of significant incidents and you were copied on notices, and Mr. Coric was also copied, and you were the only one copied from the crime investigative services, for those types of events, would you have cause to speak to Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Crime Police Department of the Mostar Centre, so I had a hierarchy to respect. My superior was Mr. Marcinko and later on the battalion commander, and we drafted all our reports in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I do one more document before the break? This is P03209. It's the same section. P03209. If you go back, section 2. Mr. Usher. 3209, thank you. This is July 5th.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a July 5th report from Mr. Bozic at the Heliodrom, and in it he reports that on July 5th, at 1.00 that morning, "... bursts were fired at the windows of the halls and the school where detainees were accommodated. The shooting lasted until 3.00, and the perpetrators are our unidentified soldiers ..." He says that: "... the commander, Mile Pusic, the brigade police, and the military police at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering were informed immediately about this incident. An agreement was reached that the brigade police should stop the incident. And according to the deputy commander of the prison military police, Kozul, this was not done, and the shooting stopped after some time without police intervention." So, sir, at this point in July, this letter was copied to you, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Coric, and Mr. Pusic. And at this point, on July 5th, your office is at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you remember this incident? You have to speak.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "Not really" is somewhere between, yes and no, and I would submit to you this is a fairly significant event.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You don't remember this. And so do you have any memory of anyone from your group, investigative services, going over to the Heliodrom and investigating this?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was sent to us through the Military Police Battalion, we probably processed this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at that point, you were the head of the Military Crime Services in Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the very days when I took over from Mr. Marcinko, who fell ill, when I assumed the position of head of the military crime police in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So, further reason why an incident in your early days as being chief or lead of that group, "an early incident as unusual as this should have taken some notice." So can you tell me -- I understand you say you don't remember, but can you tell me, why is it that the Military Police Investigative Services did not investigate this?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that it didn't, because I don't remember. And we see, from this document, that the brigade was informed, and the military police at the brigade level, in keeping with the hierarchy. And probably we, from the Crime Department, were also informed, because the perpetrators were unknown soldiers. But I really don't know whether we investigated this incident, but more likely we did, if we did receive this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, so it appears that in regard to the Heliodrom, you were involved, at least at the beginning, for the registration. Is it also true that when people were released, you were involved to a certain extent of signing off that they had no criminal record and they could be released? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were requested to submit such certificates, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So we know you were involved in the beginning, you were involved at the end, but now I want to talk about in the middle and what your role was in regard to what was ongoing at Heliodrom while the prisoners remained there. Did you have any role?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So to the extent that there were incidents that took place there, were you notified, would you be involved with that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so, for example, in instances where Muslims were maltreated, there would have been a report, and would your group be notified?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so when we see documents indicating maltreatment and you're copied, should we understand that criminal investigations resulted from those notifications?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took action upon such notifications, and that action was within our jurisdiction or remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So from July to December of 1993, were you notified that prisoners at the Heliodrom were being taken out to work and were either killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the prisoners being taken out to work, apart from the detainees whom we processed. I was notified about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So if you were notified about the detainees who might have been wounded or killed because they were within your sector, is it your position that any time we see documents of your notification, that would regard those HVO Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. I believe I have to clarify. Mr. Stanko Bozic wrote to me, among others, all the time. From early July, he constantly informed me, among other persons, no matter whether it was about those under the jurisdiction of our Crime Department, whom we processed, or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So just so I am clear, it's your testimony that when you were notified by Stanko Bozic that people had been taken from the Heliodrom and had been wounded or killed, those people could either have been HVO detainees, Muslim detainees, or they could have been Muslim civilians; you don't know, but it could be either category?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as a result of receiving those notifications, would you conduct investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from conducting investigations, if we knew certain names important for those investigations, we would also check whether, among those names, there was someone whom we had processed for criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as part of the reason that -- in regard to all these notifications, as part of the reason that you don't know whether those people were either HVO Muslim detainees or Muslim civilians, is it because the Heliodrom was randomly sending people out for labour without any system in place?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which persons that's about unless I'm given the names. So if I'm given a general report, without names, I cannot really form an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to look at now binder 3. This is a different binder. It's binder 3, and it comes in two parts. Specifically, we're going to look at part 1. There we go. Sir, this is -- in part 1 are 66 documents, dated from July 4th through December 14th, where you were given notice that prisoners were being taken from the Heliodrom for work and they were either wounded or killed. And for the record, it's not the Prosecution's position that this is the universe of documents reflecting that during that period of time. These are just the documents in regard -- that are copied to Mr. Vidovic. So this is 66 documents. That's 24 weeks' worth of documents where, if we average it out, you were notified at least -- or almost three times a week of these deaths and woundings. Mr. Vidovic, would you agree with me that this was a big problem for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this was not a problem that could go unnoticed by you or your superiors, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now if we go to part 2 of that binder, so it's the second half, these are additional documents, and these documents are not in numerical order. They go by date. They start in July, they go through November, and what these are is -- yes, thank you. The first document will be the order to send people out for labour, and then the document right behind it is going to be the report on the woundings or killings. So we're going to look at the very first one, 3253. This appears -- it's July 7th, signed by Jelic. It appears to be what I would term as a pro forma document, and it's requesting labour. And we've seen this type of document several times. Have you ever seen this type of document before, 3253?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. Have you ever seen this type of document before? Maybe not this particular one, but --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are documents signed by the commander of the defence of the city. I don't remember having seen these documents in going about the work of our department.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But if you'll bear with me, as a police officer and a lawyer, I think you have some ability to talk about this document with me. Sir, you'll see here, in a second paragraph, it has the person, there's a line, they fill in the blank, "... is personally responsible for taking over the prisoners for their security and welfare while they will be carrying out public works ..." And then in parentheses it has: "(Cleaning of the streets, parks, settlements, and premises)." And below that, it says: "The prisoners are to be treated in accordance with the International Humanitarian Law and Geneva Conventions." Mr. Vidovic, are you aware that International Humanitarian Law allows certain status of prisoners to do work, as long as it's not related to military operations, and the work that they can do is illustrated by this very document, this public works? Are you aware of that law?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you're aware that prisoners are not allowed to do work related to the conduct of military operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that part of the reason that they're allowed to do public work, cleaning the streets, parks, settlements, premises, part of the reason that they're allowed to do that is that is considered to be safe work, as opposed to military operations? Do you agree that's a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Because in some places, in places where they would be carrying on military operations, in those places there is a distinct possibility that these prisoners could be wounded or killed; does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if, for example, civilians had been taken out to do work related to military operations, that would have been a crime for which you were responsible to investigate; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said "civilians"?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our work, we exclusively dealt with military staff, military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if a military person came in and took some civilians out to do work related to military operations, would you be obligated to investigate that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's look at the next document right behind it. It's P03293, P03293. And this is the corresponding report to this order. So based on this order -- this request for 40 prisoners, they were sent out, and these 40 detainees were given for labour, with the approval of Mr. Pusic. And on their return from labour: " ... we were informed that one of the detainees ... was wounded by the BH Army and was transferred to the hospital ..." Sir, do you remember looking into this incident where 40 prisoners were actually sent out to do work and one of them was wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were indirectly involved in such cases, through military units and their security structures, that is, the SIS at brigade level, who had jurisdiction over them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this report is copied to you, but you don't have any memory of this -- of any investigation that your group conducted here; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, based on this document, but I repeat that we conducted certain investigations into such cases; I mean, our service.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that in a situation where one of the prisoners was wounded by the BH Army, so in this case the enemy of the HVO, it might give you an indication that these people were working in a situation that had to do with something -- something to do with military operations?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must once again mention that all of Mostar was a war zone. The entire city was a dangerous war zone, where there was daily shelling, and you must know that even far away from the front-line people were killed or wounded by snipers daily. In the area where my house is, and that is some 700 or 800 metres away from the front-line, even there people were killed by snipers; that is to say, in other words, that all of Mostar was a war zone. So we cannot speak about parks being safe places.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Then let's talk specifically about HVO positions. Let's go to P03766, and you're going to see it just a couple more documents back. 03766. This is August 9th. This document is a request for 20 detainees by the commander of the 2nd Battalion, Puljic. And then you go to the very next document, 4221, and this is the corresponding report in regard to these 20 prisoners. Sir, in this request, it says: "You are requested to place 20 detainees at our disposal to do the necessary works on fortifying our positions." Now, would you agree with me that "fortifying our positions" is clearly related to military operations?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I am not sure which document we're reading now, 4221 or another. I got lost because the interpreter interpreted that into Croatian, but the transcript shows something else. The transcript reads "in the report," whereas it was interpreted "you say." But none of these documents originates from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, which document are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The first one, which is P03766. It's the corresponding request, the first one, 3766. This is the request from Mr. Puljic, and he says: "You are requested to place 20 detainees at our disposal to do the necessary works on fortifying our position."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. West, in my document, I read "25."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Thank you, Your Honour, "25 detainees."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Possibly my learned friend is reading from the wrong document, because this doesn't say "fortifying our positions." It says "perform urgent tasks for the needs of," et cetera, and that's document 3766. So this may not be the right document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think it is my mistake, and I'll go back to it. Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, in these -- generally during that period of time, when you were notified that people were killed or wounded, you've testified that in some cases you started investigations. Tell the Trial Chamber how you discerned which cases you started investigations on and which cases you did not.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me generally, not related to this document, so your question doesn't refer to this particular document, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our investigations were instigated if we received written reports containing information that the persons mentioned there can be found in our files. In such cases, we were duty-bound to act and inform the Military Prosecutor's Office accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, we're going to stay in the same binder, but we're going to go to the part before, part 1, and talk about these 66 reports.
