When you just said "our investigations were instigated if we received written reports containing information," I would submit to you this is 66 times where you're receiving a written report indicating these deaths and wounded. And if we go through these, and you can take a moment to look at some of these, there are more than 66, but many of them go to you, I would submit to you that in these reports, they don't indicate whether these people are detainees, whether they are civilians, whether they're ABiH prisoners of war, they just give names. And, sir, would you agree with me that the reason that Bozic is just giving you names of people and not giving you status is because he didn't know the status? Sir, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he knew. It was his business to know. But as I said, he wrote to me all the time, whether it had to do with us or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right, sir. If it's your testimony that you conducted investigations when you received notice of the status of the person killed or wounded, are you telling this Trial Chamber that above and beyond these 66 documents copied to you, you received other documents, other reports, indicating that the persons wounded or killed were HVO -- or, rather, were people under your control? Is that what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said -- I apologise for interrupting the Prosecutor, but on page 48 the witness said that, "we launch investigations when we received written reports which contained information." And then as far as I understood him -- I would like the witness to be given an opportunity to clarify, because only half of what he said is being interpreted. Why doesn't he clarify which registry -- registers or files he was referring to, because he said several times over that upon receiving such reports, he would check his files. I believe that he's trying to say something, but doesn't have the chance to say it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This could be an additional question. But if the transcript does not faithfully reflect what the witness has said, it is better for the witness to clarify this. So, Witness, what did you say, exactly? And this should not be deducted from the time of questions posed by or put by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said -- the way it was, these were our registers or files, namely, the files of the Crime Department, where I worked, and which were made only for the use of our Crime Department for the cases we were working on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, as this has been interrupted anyway, I would like to put to you what I consider a basic question. Did you ever, ever start an investigation after you had received a report that persons taken from Heliodrom to work had been killed or wounded? Did that ever trigger an investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, if the persons involved were detainees processed by our department. If the persons involved were disarmed HVO members, the investigation was conducted by the brigade, that is, the security structures of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I was actually asking whether you, the Military Police Crime Prosecution Department, started any such investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely what I want to explain to you. We did if we had the authority over the person; that is to say, if before we were processing him for another criminal offence. And there were cases when such detainees, too, without permission from the prosecution or informing us within our legal frameworks, would be taken out to do labour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be possible for you to give any examples for this? Do you recall any specific cases of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the break I believe we saw a document where that note, the famous note, was mentioned where certain soldiers were being handed over, people against whom a criminal report had been filed for murder. If you remember the slip, there was a slip there with a text and Tuta's signature, where there were three civilians being taken -- three soldiers being taken and one civilian. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, I hope I didn't mess up your plan, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please listen carefully. There were 56 people killed and 191 people injured, and that's as far as I can recollect, which means that, in total, there were over 200 cases of people who were either wounded or killed during the period in question; namely, where they were detained at the Heliodrom. Out of those roughly 200 cases, as far as you can recollect, how many investigations did you launch? This is just a rough figure. One, five, ten, twenty, fifty, what figure could you give? Because I can understand that you cannot give the name of a victim. This can be understood. Seventeen years down the line, who would be able to do that? However, you may be in a position to remember as to whether there were five, ten, twenty, thirty, or fifty investigations that were launched. That could be possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I can answer that by giving a figure, but I do know that investigations were conducted. But I really can't give you a number because, after all, it's been 17 years, and I don't have those classifications in my mind now, within criminal reports, to be able to know a definite number and so on. It's difficult for me to do that, Your Honour, so I don't think I can answer your question by giving you any figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, of these 66 reports to you giving you notice, there are 19 reports where notice went to you and to Mr. Coric as well, and there are 9 reports where notice went to you and Mr. Pusic as well. Upon receipt of these reports, did you speak to Mr. Coric about them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: As I said a moment ago, Mr. Bozic would write to me non-stop. I kept getting --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I appreciate that and we have heard it, but my question is quite clear and it requires a yes or no. It can be, Yes; it can be, No; it can be, I don't know. When you received these reports, the ones where Mr. Coric was copied, did you have a discussion with him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether I talked to Coric; is that it? Instead of talking to him, I wrote to him, to Mr. Coric, and I asked that at meetings of the Military Police Administration, finally our department, from top level, be allowed to do our work, as it says in our heading and title, "Department for the Prevention and Investigation of Crime." And I think that sometime toward the end of July, at a meeting at the military police, a decision was taken which was sent on down to me through the battalion, because I wasn't at the meeting, it was the commander battalion who attended the meeting, and I think that it was precisely this written decision where Mr. Coric, the chief, was taking on board what I had requested, was giving me permission. And after that, I think that I personally gave a copy to Mr. Bozic of that decision. I handed it to him personally, I think, and asked him not to keep writing to me about matters that didn't come under my remit, but that he should contact the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's talk about an example, one we just spoke about 15 minutes ago. In a situation where you receive notice that an HVO military commander came in, took out detainees, and that these detainees are civilians, and that some of those civilians were wounded or killed, and you receive notice of that, are you telling us that you did an investigation and a prosecution resulted from that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And are you telling us that Mr. Coric told you to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why Coric? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You, yourself, did an investigation, transferred it over to the prosecution, and prosecutions resulted?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vidovic, I've not seen any documents that look anything like that. And in your direct testimony with counsel, we have not seen any documents that look like that either. Are you suggesting that at the time there's documents supporting this notion, but you haven't seen any recently?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember a very interesting case from the sphere of what you're talking about. We had a situation - I think it was in July 1993 - in which an organised group of HVO soldiers right up at the front-line, in Ricina Street, was mistreating people and forcing them out of their flats. And since it was the front-line, and since that came under the direct authority of the commander of the defence of the town, Mr. Jelic, I personally informed him of that case, the one which we received information about, that it had happened, and then a group was organised under the command of Mr. Jelic directly which assisted us, arrested these soldiers, and we processed them and filed criminal reports. I think that was July 1993 in Ricina Street. And they were members of the HVO who were up at the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell me their names, and were they convicted?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't do that. Perhaps if I were to see a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, let's look at P03518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to get back to a question which was put to you by Ms. West. As far as civilians are concerned, you come from a country where the law is being applied, and it is applied with precision. We had a witness before you who explained to us that the civilian prison had been transferred to the Heliodrom. We can, therefore, conclude that at the Heliodrom there are also civilian prisoners. A civilian prisoner, unless I'm mistaken - and if I make a mistake, please correct me, because you're a lawyer - comes under the civilian authority, the civilian court, and may serve a sentence that has been handed down by civilian jurisdiction, unless we are talking about civilians that have been involved in cases that fall within the authority of the military prosecutor or other authorities. Based on that, a civilian who leaves the Heliodrom, as far as you know, does this civilian, according to what Ms. West is saying, fall under the authority of the military police and the military prosecutor or can this civilian fall under the authority of the civilian authorities, i.e., the civilian -- civil investigating judge who has imprisoned him, the civil court, and the civil prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean the case I quoted earlier on, I think it was Mr. Klemo, and it was the crime of murder, but he was a civilian, so he comes under civilian authority and jurisdiction. But from the prison, he was taken out by a military personnel, taking him to a military operation. But at the point of his arrival at Heliodrom and while he was in Heliodrom, he was a civilian, pursuant to a decision -- put there following a decision by a civilian court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military who took him out of the prison, did they know what his legal position was exactly, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what they knew about the legal position. But the persons who were taken out and who were under the authority of our department, we informed the military prosecutor about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My last question now. You have noticed, as I have, and Ms. West pointed this out to you, and I thank her for that, that the orders were all the same; it was just a matter of filling in the empty boxes. But you filled in the empty boxes by writing figures in there, We need 20 detainees, but there was no difference between the civilians, prisoners of war, and the others. As far as you know, don't you think this could be a source of confusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it wasn't I who was doing this filling out. I didn't ask for those people, nor did I condone it. There were exceptional cases in which I could give those who were being processed by us, but then they would contact me, I would ask permission from the prosecutor or investigating judge, and then I would act. But that was a matter of mere logistics, nothing more. As to all the rest, I did not take part in any of this giving of people for labour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I still want to stick with that example with the four -- I don't think they were murderers; they were suspected murderers, probably. Do you recall whether any of these was wounded or killed while out working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean of the four, or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Of these four.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think they were harmed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In that case --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... or killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, in that case, the example fails. When I asked you for examples of prosecution, I was thinking of cases where persons -- prisoners, detainees, I use this un-technically, were taken to work and were killed or wounded. That was what I meant might have called for an investigation. And I wanted to know whether, in any such cases, you had an example where there had actually been an investigation. And so far, it seems we still have no example for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember one example very characteristic for what you're asking me about and saying, Your Honour. And with your permission, I'll tell you about it. During the war operations in July 1993, from the detention in Heliodrom, taken out was -- and I think I'll be right in saying -- 99 per cent right if I say that just like that famous slip we were looking at, something was taken for the needs or requirements of an operation -- or, rather, a member of the HVO was taken out. I can't remember his name now, but I know that he was not from Mostar and that he was a Serb. He was killed in the war operations, and our department carried out a full investigation and handed the entire report over to -- we handed over the entire report and criminal report to the criminal prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his last sentence, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had an opportunity to meet him just before this act. When he was taken over from Heliodrom and when we learnt about his death, our department launched an investigation. He was in Mostar alone. He wasn't from Mostar, himself, and he had nobody close to him in Mostar. And I remember that we spent a long time looking for anyone who knew him, and all that we learnt was that he was from Western Bosnia, Prijedor or thereabouts. So that, Your Honour, would be an example of what we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you recall what the result of the investigation was? Was anybody identified as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting. I was waiting patiently to say something linked to what my learned friend said; that we, during these proceedings, have not seen documents showing that something had been reported to the prosecutor. What I want to say is that, unfortunately, during this trial we did not receive from the prosecutor a single binder from any prosecutor's office in Bosnia-Herzegovina, neither civilian nor military, and the Defence of Mr. Coric earlier on - I'm sure Their Honours will remember - during the Prlic Defence case, along with the witness, introduced some CDs with books from the prosecution. However, they were just books about cases registered. Neither the OTP nor us -- we weren't able to access any complete documentation from all the prosecutor's offices and military courts. And just like in this Military District Court in Mostar and the military prosecutor in Mostar, that was the case there too. That's my first point. Now, my second point is: Unfortunately, in this trial, because it doesn't exist in the Croatian archives, did we manage to access the incoming and outgoing registration books, and the incoming and outgoing registration books of the military police of the HVO, and I think -- nor SIS, either, so that I think that nobody can claim in this trial either that they've seen all the documents or that they will see them by the end of this trial. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, in answer to Judge Trechsel's question, you gave us one example of an investigation, and this is one example on the face of 66 notifications to you that there have been people killed or wounded. Sir, I put it to you that the general HVO policy at the time was not to investigate these cases at all, and my question is: Is this because the HVO did not think it was a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer on behalf of the entire HVO. As far as the department that I worked in, we considered that every criminal report and every crime committed should -- that a criminal report should be filed against the perpetrator of those crimes and acts.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you please look at P03518. So this is in part 1 of the binder you're in.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask the interpreters to speak up, because I hear the Prosecutor louder than I hear the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 3518, 3518. There you go. This is July 17th. This is a report. You were copied, Mr. Coric, and Mr. Pusic: "On July 16th, three detainees were supplied to work at recovering the bodies of our soldiers who had been killed on the order of Mr. Ivica Pisic ..." And: " ... with the approval of Mr. Berislav Pusic, the control officer." And then it lists the detainees. Mr. Vidovic, recovering bodies of soldiers is, of course, related to the conduct of military operations, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that this particular case was not investigated, it was not sent over for prosecution, and no conviction resulted?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. And here, from the document, we can see that mention is made of the SIS of the brigade, and the brigade police is also mentioned, so these are persons who came under their domain. I state, once again, I cannot exclude the fact that an investigation was launched later on by our department. But looking at this document, I can't know that, I don't know that. All I can see from this document is that it is an internal document from Heliodrom, informing about the activities of the 3rd Brigade. And I have to add that the 3rd Brigade was located and put up at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want you to assume for me the following: Assume that there's an influx of well over 2.000 prisoners into Heliodrom in the month of July, that a substantial part of those people are civilians, that they're mixed together with other people who are detained at that facility, that the prison officials who run the place don't know who's who, they don't know who's a civilian, they don't know who's an HVO Muslim soldier, they don't know who is an ABiH prisoner of war, and they don't know who is a real HVO detainee, that these people are subject to a system whereby HVO military people come in, and without any rules or regulations, they go ahead and they take whomever they want for labour, without anyone in the prison and without any of those people coming in knowing the status of who is going out. Mr. Vidovic, would you agree with me that this is a system that might occasion civilians ending up going to do forced labour in military operations?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with your assumption, but once again I have to repeat, for the umpteenth time, what my role was in all this. I was a crime investigator of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so do I take it that you are not -- it's your position that you can't answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. The question -- if I may have the mike. The question was answered, and the Prosecutor is now being unfair to the witness. And there's no need to be unfair to the witness. He did -- perhaps she wasn't listening or didn't get quite the answer that she wanted, but he did indicate, it's very clear: "I can agree with your assumption." You posed a hypothetical, an assumption, and he said: "I can agree with that." But then he went on to stress his role. So you did get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He did, in fact, answer. I have a question after you, Mr. Ibrisimovic. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't want to interrupt my learned friend when she showed the document 3515 [as interpreted], but the identical situation was with other documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the number slowly, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And looking at paragraph 13, Mr. Pusic at that time was not a liaison officer. I beg your pardon, I mean control officer. But according to the 5th of July submission, he was appointed head of the Service for Prisoner Exchange, and I'm saying this for the record. The documents were P3518 and document P3293 and P345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on looking at the last document, 3518, P3518, could the following situation have occurred: Since the Heliodrom is a military prison where a soldier is being sanctioned by the military authority by his brigade commander, and he is taken into custody, and he serves a 15-day custody sentence -- every person having done his military service knows exactly what this means. So this person is in the Heliodrom, and then, lo and behold, his unit wants to recover him because they want him to perform labour. He does not report to the military prosecutor and he doesn't report to the military police either, because he has been sanctioned as part of the disciplinary measures, and his unit want to recover him because they want him to perform labour, and he is killed in circumstances we are not familiar with, since the document doesn't mention these. The investigation that is going to be conducted -- well, should this investigation be conducted by the SIS of his brigade, or the military police of the brigade, and perhaps even by yourself, afterwards if it so happens that an offence has been committed? Can you spell this out for us, because we are discussing extremely complex matters and you can help us understand the situation better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the example you have just given in the first part has to do with disciplinary proceedings which the unit commander launched against his soldier. I must tell you that these disciplinary proceedings -- or, rather, soldiers who were sanctioned for disciplinary breaches by their commanders also served their sentences, say 15 days, at the Heliodrom; that is, in the building where detainees were because of whom we went to the Heliodrom daily or according to need. If an incident as described by you should occur, namely, that the commander takes a detainee out of detention while he's serving his sentence, and I believe that you said the detainee got killed, well, our department didn't process such cases. They were -- they came under the exclusive jurisdiction of the SIS of the brigade, or the brigade generally speaking. We were not faced with such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think I was right in asking the question. Ms. West, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, you spoke earlier about the reasons why post-June 30th that Muslim men were arrested. You said that they were arrested because they were Muslim, and the concern was because they were Muslim, their allegiance would be to the ABiH, and not the HVO. So I'd like to look at P11237, and we're now in binder 2, which I think is a different binder than what you have in front of you. Binder 2 has two parts, part 1 and part 2. Thank you. We're going to go to P11237. Okay. And this is July 11th, 1993, and it's to you, it's a request to you. And it says: "The following soldiers have joined and proved to be loyal to the HVO since the beginning of the conflict with the Serb aggression as well as in the latest conflict with the ABiH." And, We are requesting their release. Mr. Vidovic, do you remember receiving requests like this?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the rare requests which was also sent directly to me. I mentioned a short while ago, you may remember, about -- something about logistics, and within logistics, let's say the Pioneers. I remember an incident where an auxiliary road was built, it was under construction, as a route from Mostar to Siroki Brijeg, because the existing road that had been there before the war was constantly being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sure what you're saying is relevant to this. But just in a general way, you'll agree with me that sometimes you receive requests to release?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in this case, these two soldiers, by their names, can you tell their ethnicity or their nationality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are Muslims by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And these people were released because it appeared to be clear that their allegiance was not to the ABiH and it, in fact, was to the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I must add that the person mentioned under 2, Mr. Drljevic, was the subject of an investigation of ours for theft, so he was under our jurisdiction at the Heliodrom. Senad Drljevic, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So, sir, you were involved in sort of a logistical way in the releases of people from Heliodrom; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when people were released, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to this document, or is it a general question?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be seen here that they could go home or they could leave Mostar, wherever they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's talk about some different people. We're going to go to P03008. It's that binder, but it's the second part, 3008. This is dated June 29th.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's marked as "3008" here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is June 29th, and this is an early document. This is even before the June 30 round-up. But it says -- it's from you, it's to the Heliodrom, and it asks the administration to hand over the following prisoners. It lists eight. And it says: "The aforementioned prisoners will leave for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at their own demand." So in this case, these particular people were leaving Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if prisoners were willing to leave Herceg-Bosna, was that a way they could get out of prison?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a rule, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to go to P03616. It should just be a couple more. And this is a meeting from July 21. And for the record, I'll note, we talked about this yesterday, it had a different exhibit number, it was a different translation, and that -- from yesterday, the parties were using 5D04115. Today, we have 3616. This is a meeting that you attended. You spoke about this yesterday, and these are the minutes, so I want to focus on this. And we're going to look at the bottom of English page 2 to 3, and it's the part right under your name. And it says: "If we (as we were charged to do) had carried out the round-up of inhabitants in the town, it should not have happened that a unit or group started rounding up people in the town." And then you cite an example. You say that: "The police from the Pupils' Hall of Residence, who of their own bat, rounded up the inhabitants in one quarter of town and drove them out of their flats which they then looted and carried off items. The Welfare Centre is the institution to draw up a list of people who want to emigrate to abroad, and why should we dispute that with them?" Mr. Vidovic, at the beginning of this passage, Judge Trechsel asked you about this, the part that says: " ... if we, as we were charged to do, had carried out the roundup of the inhabitants in town ..." And, sir, is it your testimony that the military police was not involved with the round-up of the residents?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said yesterday, once I had seen this document, if I remember well, that this was not a transcript, but rather that the minutes were signed by one Javorka Ribica. This is a document of the MUP, the civilian police. I saw this document for the first time yesterday, and I decidedly claim that I did not say that. So this is about the meeting the purpose of which was enhancing crime enforcement in co-operation with the civilian and the military police, the Military Court and the Prosecutor's Office. We saw that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to move on, because I'm not going to focus on that right now. But I'm going to focus on the part that says: "The Welfare Centre is the institution to draw up a list of people who want to emigrate to abroad, and why should we dispute that with them?" Sir, you were familiar with this practice of the Welfare Centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My department, where I worked, had contacts with the Social Welfare Centre, and pursuant to the orders received from the zone of operations -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you were familiar with this practice of drawing up this list, this list they had?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know what the centre promised those people in return for them to leave?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you think one of the reasons that these people were willing to go abroad was perhaps because their flats were being looted and items carried off?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prefer to look at things from a different angle. There was a war on in Mostar, and the state of war had been in place since April 1992. The living conditions were unbearable for the vast majority of the inhabitants of the town, irrespective of their religious or ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there and ask you: This list that the Welfare Centre drew up, do you understand that the people primarily on that list were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Which list are we talking about? Does the witness know that at all? I cannot see any list in front of me, so I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think the witness understands what I'm referring to, and it's what's in this document, page 3, at the top: "The Welfare Centre is the institution to draw up a list of people who want to emigrate ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vidovic, you've indicated that the people primarily on the list were Muslim. If we can go down on the English page towards the bottom, under "Velimir Maric, president of the District Military Court." And underneath Mr. Maric, it says: "We are in a serious war for Croatian territory. Without unity, the Croats will lose the war." Now, Mr. Vidovic, you were at this meeting, and you heard this discussion. Would you agree with me that part of the way to win the war for what was here named Croatian territory was to get rid of the Muslims? Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was it a practice to send Muslims to third countries to get them out of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any practice involving the organised sending of Muslims to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Then let's talk about it the way you have, organised sending of Muslims to third countries. Were you involved in that procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's go to page 4 of the English, and it's the next occasion where you speak, where the words are attributed to you. It says: "The Defence Department invited me to be present as host for the American attache's visit to the Heliodrom in Mostar, which they want to put on a show and compare it with Manjaca. I think that we have to stop bringing Muslims into the Heliodrom. In the days to come, we will help those people leave the town for the Republic of Croatia and abroad as soon as possible." So let me ask you again, sir. Were you involved in that organisation of sending Muslims to third countries?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat, No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But at this point, you won't deny that many Muslims were sent to third countries or sent out of Herceg-Bosna to another country; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, many people from Mostar - Croats, Muslims, and Serbs - were leaving Mostar because the war was raging in Mostar. So we cannot say that only a certain ethnic group was leaving Mostar. You must know that at that time the entire Adriatic Coast was flooded with refugees who were put up in hotels, and those refugees were from Bosnia-Herzegovina. They fled from the war because there was a war on in Mostar. People were being killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But what we're focus on right now is the lists that were created by the Welfare Centre, and you've already agreed that those lists comprised Muslim people, not Croats and not Serbs. Those lists comprised Muslim people and that there was an organisation in place to remove them to third countries. I would like to go to P03572 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I asked you this question before on this point, but Ms. West is right in putting the question again. The document that we have before us is an incriminating document, if we take this into account. You intervene in this discussion to say that there is the American attache's visit, so we can understand what this could mean; he's going to look at what's happening. And then you say: "I think that we have to stop bringing Muslims into the Heliodrom ..." And then you say: "... we have to help those people leave the town for the Republic of Croatia and abroad as soon as possible." So you can see what is happening, and this is what Ms. West is putting to you. Sir, you have challenged this. I'm trying to place this in the context on how things unfolded. In this document, it is obvious that all participants are talking about the crime trends; murders, unrest, and so on and so forth. And you are taking the floor after the military prosecutor, who is not talking about sending away Muslims to the outside, but to start proceedings, and you're taking the floor just after him. So I was wondering whether you were not tempted to say that all those people that are subject of criminal investigations, as it happened in Cuba when they send away their criminals to the United States, you are in favour for those Muslims to all leave. Did you have that in mind, or, as far as you were concerned, you had to go to the next step and making sure that all Muslims from Mostar were leaving the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my reply I could repeat that this is not a transcript, but rather minutes that I saw for the first time yesterday. I disagree with what is said on page 2 and also what's said on page 3. This was a meeting called by the civilian police, and it only had one topic; namely, crime. I attended with my colleagues from the department. And I repeat once more that I didn't take part in the making of any lists or nor was I involved in the organising of the departures of persons to third countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand you correctly, you are saying that this is not a transcript, but these are words that were lent to you, and it was taken by somebody else, so you don't agree with this informal transcript, and you did not take part in the departure of those Muslims to other countries. This is what we have to understand from what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P03572. Do you have that, sir? Thank you. This is an order from you, and it's July 19th, and this is another order -- and it says: "You are instructed to release from Heliodrom the person under the name," it gives the name, "who is right now at work in the ATG or the Convicts Battalion. The person mentioned above will be taken over and taken to his apartment by the commander of the ATG, Martinovic, and he has been put on a list of persons who are going to leave abroad for the Office of Refugees at HZ-HB." So, sir, in this particular case, although you have testified that you were not involved in the organisation of the departure of people, here it appears that you were ordering the release of a prisoner at the Heliodrom to go abroad; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document, the one that you're showing to me now, I received a request to look into the criminal responsibility, and those requests arrived through the Heliodrom, and this type of written document I would return to the Heliodrom. So this was just one such document, one of the documents needed so that, through the centre, these people should be released. So all this is about is record-keeping.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. Vidovic. And I'm not suggesting that you had a say on who goes on the Welfare Centre list. I don't think that's the case. I think, as you've said, you're involved in the process and the facilitation. You agree with me that that was the case? You helped move these people along, you didn't put them on the list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. My role in all this was to issue certain permits and certificates from our department --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't want you to repeat. And if you don't understand my question, you can say that, but my question requires a, Yes, No, or, I don't know. But let's just move on in this document. I think it would be helpful. At the very bottom on 3572, it says: "He has not been returned. Stela took over, and took home." Mr. Vidovic, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting it is. I just want to know what it means. Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't wish to speculate. All that I can say is that I returned this through the battalion with a stamp, I sent it back with a stamp, so this paper was sent to Heliodrom through our regular channels. Now, this addition in handwriting, I don't want to speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'm going to tell you what I think it means, and I'm going to ask you a question. This indicates that when they went looking for this Haris Tanovic, he wasn't at the work site for the Convicts Battalion, and he had not been -- excuse me, he had not been returned to the Heliodrom. And whoever wrote this indicated that, instead, Stela took over and took him home. So, in fact, the commander took this Muslim prisoner and took him home. If that's the case, Mr. Vidovic, that would be a crime, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that we issued from our records that, from the aspects of crime, he was of no interest to us, so I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I'm going to decline to accept that answer, because it's not responsive. My question was: If this commander took this Muslim prisoner home with him, that would be a crime, correct? And that would be a crime that you would be obligated to investigate.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we had knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, sir, you did have knowledge of it. It's written on the paper, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point. Let's look at the transcript. Perhaps my learned colleague is not listening to the answers that she's getting. The gentleman indicated that that's not his handwriting. He indicated that he doesn't know who put the handwriting there. He indicated that he signed it, and then it went off to put a stamp, and then the document went afterwards someplace where somebody put that writing on the document itself. Now we've come full circle and now we're accusing the gentleman of lying, essentially, or at least trying to cover up his tracks, when he's indicated all along that he never saw the handwriting on the document before he signed it and he didn't see the document after he signed it. And never mind the fact that she posed a hypothetical based on facts which are really not in evidence. Supposedly, this is what this means. We don't know, we don't have any evidence. But I didn't object at that point in time, because I took that to mean a general question, If somebody were to take somebody home, would that be a crime? As a general nature, I accept the answer, fine. But now to say that this gentleman knew about it and didn't do anything, that is stretching it, it's going beyond the facts in this case, and I would object.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll move on. That document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, perhaps you did not understand the questions that were put to you. We have a document dealing with someone called Haris Tanovic. It seems that this person, Haris Tanovic, is working with the Convicts Battalion. And you are saying -- because this is your document, it's a document you drafted, you are saying that this person has to be taken over, taken to his apartment by Colonel Martinovic, also known as Stela, and then you say: "Haris Tanovic has been put on the list of persons who are going to leave abroad through the Office for Refugees." And then you sign this document. Ms. West has put the following question to you, and it's her point of view, of course, but she's asking for your point of view. She was wondering whether the fact that you take someone to his apartment and then you send him abroad is a crime. This is a question that she's put to you. What do you answer to this very question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't really answer that, I can't give a yes-or-no answer. It's very specific. Your Honour, what I write here, well, I get a request in this same form, and the request was to release from Heliodrom Tanovic, to check out his connections to the Crime Department and the fact that he is presently with the Convicts Battalion and will be taken over by such and such, and that he's been included on the list. So I'm just copying that out and sending it to Heliodrom. So I don't know whether there were elements indicating that a crime had been committed, nor do I know what was handwritten there and what happened later. This is a document sent to Heliodrom, and afterwards I received no feedback information about this. So it's difficult for me to answer and say whether it was, in fact, a crime or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, what I don't understand is why you were involved in this process in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this: We were duty-bound, on orders from the operative zone, to issue certificates, as the Crime Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I understand better. In other words, if this person or individual was the subject of an investigation, you would have then stood in the way of his departure; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we were conducting an investigation at that point in time, then, yes. In any other situation, the person would have no interest, as far as we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, I have understood. Ms. West, maybe she has understood also. You have the floor. My colleague has just told me that it is time to have a break. We shall have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I inquire as to the time remaining?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecution has used 2 hours and 5 minutes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, we're going to go to P03527. It's binder 2, part 2, so I think you're right there. 3527. Is that binder 2? 3527. Mr. Usher, my apologies, but if you could provide some assistance, I think ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this is July 18th, it's your report, and it's about events on July 17th. This is a special report about the work of the branch office, and we're going to go all the way to the last paragraph, number 4: "Yesterday evening at 2300 hours, the branch office assisted the Office for Expelled Persons in the HZ-HB. In the organisation the first group who voluntarily left Mostar, departed from the place in front of the military police building and left for third countries. 500 persons departed in 9 buses." Mr. Vidovic, these 500 people left from in front of your building; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left from in front of the zone that our building is located in; that is to say, the area of the Mechanical Engineering Faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And these are the people who, as you called it, were -- there was an organisation by which to send them to third countries. These are 500 of those people; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And they are all Muslim, are they not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this position, I can't say whether all 500 were Muslims or not. All I can do is to clarify what we were doing within this option.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's go to P03617. It's in the same part of that binder, 3617. This is a letter from exiled citizens of Mostar temporarily sheltered at the refugee camp, and this is a letter that they put together regarding their expulsion from Mostar. And specifically we're going to go to paragraph 4 in the English, and it says: "Prisoners, camp inmates, and concentration camp inmates who assigned with the HVO and the Department for Social Welfare of the so-called Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna that they would leave Mostar with their families at their own will, and only half an hour to three hours to prepare themselves for departure and to gather at the agreed meeting place at the University of Mostar, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering." Mr. Vidovic, these are the people --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I apologise, but perhaps my colleague misunderstood, but this isn't a letter from people leaving Mostar, or we received the wrong interpretation. What this is, is a piece of information compiled by two individuals, and we can see that it is some kind of meeting that was held in front of the Embassy of the Republic of Herzegovina. Somebody attended the meeting. So I don't know what the role of these two persons signing the document is, but it's not a letter from the people themselves. That's what I wanted to point out.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But what I want to focus on is the mention of the Department for Social Welfare. This is the department or the centre we spoke about earlier and which you testified this department created lists, and on those lists were just Muslim names; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the 500 people, I said that I wasn't sure if all 500 were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, and that's my mistake. What I am asking you about is earlier we spike the list that the centre made. And it's your testimony that the list that the centre made, or the Department of Social Welfare, were comprised of Muslim people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And number 5 says they departed Mostar on July 18th. So, sir, you will agree with me that on July 17th we had the departure of 500 people that you spoke of in your report, and then July 18th we have the departure of another 500 people, as reflected here, and these people are departing from in front of the Mechanical Engineering building. Mr. Vidovic, your role in their departure to third countries, as you testified, was to ensure that they didn't have any criminal -- outstanding criminal investigations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for how many people who were departing for third countries did you do this, did you run this check?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you a number, because I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was it more than 1.000, more than 2.000? Can you give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate. I just can't speak about numbers. It's been too much time since then. And it's a sensitive matter, so I don't want to guess or speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, then we won't talk about the numbers. But let's talk about the names. Would you agree with me that the checks you did were of all Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We carried out various checks in our department, and a large number of checks for people who were Muslim too.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, you testified on Monday regarding the crimes that the military police investigated, and we spent much of Monday going through lots of documents evidencing different types of crimes that you investigated. Now -- and part of your testimony on the subject matter, and I'll ask you this, was to show that there was a working rule of law for the military police, or, rather, there was a system in place such that poorly-behaving military police officers did not run amok in Mostar; correct? You had a system in place?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did that to all the members of the HVO, not just the military police. We acted in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And so is it fair to say that the documents that you showed us on Monday presented a fair sampling of the types of crimes that you investigated?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I'm sure there were more investigations, but did you testify about the significant ones so that the Trial Chamber could have an understanding about the work that you did in the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm going to show you a table, and this is on Sanction. Mr. Usher, if I can have your assistance. We took all the documents that you testified in -- on Monday, I think it went into Tuesday, regarding these crimes and put them on a table, and it's two page's long. And you mentioned 56 documents. Now, we've looked at them, and it appears that several of them regard the same investigation, so what we've done is we've actually separated them per investigation. So, for example, you see right in the middle the rape and murder of a mother, this is the Besirovic [phoen] family, there's 14 documents that relate to that one investigation. So you spoke about 56 documents, but, in fact, it was really only 24 separate investigations, and of those there were eight murder investigations, there were two attempted murder investigations, there were three rapes, and there were ten thefts and robberies, and there was one assault. What I would like to do now is focus on a few of the investigations in detail. So, in specific, you spoke about an investigation regarding Mr. Prlic's bodyguards, and let's review your testimony on that. I think you will see that on the screen in front of you. This is from March 29th, and it regarded two exhibits, 2508 and 3513, and the question was: "Do you recall whether they were convicted?" And you said: "Yes, they were. I remember that." And so then you looked on to the second document, and then Judge Antonetti asked you a question. He says, and it's the bold: "When you did your job, were you not prevented from doing your job, as part of the Crime Department, regardless of the position of those individuals?" And specifically here we're talking about the fact that these individuals worked for Mr. Prlic. And your answer was: "Your Honour, we did not have any obstacles in our path, because it had to do with some kind of security. For us, they were military policemen. You will see the sequence of these dates, how these things developed, that this was done in a very short period of time. The matter had to be dealt with urgently, and that's how we treated it. Again, I say that we filed a criminal report, and in this way we concluded our work in the best way possible." "As far as you can recollect," the question from Judge Antonetti, "what sort of sentence was handed down for these individuals?" And the answer was: "I can't answer the question. I really don't know what kind of prison sentences they were sentenced to, but I do know that they were sentenced." Now, sir, when you spoke about these -- in particular, they were used, P03513, and then you also used P03508. Now this -- and we're going to go back to those. And it's binder number 1, which I don't believe you have in front of you - apologies, Mr. Usher - it's binder number 1, part 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just while we're looking at that, just a point of clarification. There's nothing in the record, nor do we ascribe to the fact that they were working for Mr. Prlic. They were assigned to protect him. There is a difference. So just a point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So it's 3508. Do you see that, sir? This is the document that you spoke about during your direct. And 1 through 4 are the names of the people -- this is your report that you wrote. But let's go all the way to the very last paragraph, and in the last paragraph it says: "I stress that during the process of detaining the men and taking the official notes, there were extremely intrusive precious by our department with a goal of obstructing the procedural and legal process which on this occasion too we persisted with." Mr. Vidovic, when you answered the President's questions, had you forgotten about this last paragraph and about what you were writing about this intrusive pressure? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember this. But when I wrote this, I had in mind certain military policemen who tried to prevent us in carrying out the job, so their friends and even their relatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. P06844. It's in the same section, P06844. This is November 24th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when I put the question to you, I didn't know that this document existed. If I had all the documents right from the start, I would be able to stream-line my questions better, but that's the way things go. In the last paragraph, the pressure exerted seem to come from your own department; in other words, from your superiors, not from members who are indicted. You do write "our department." Well, it's very good of you to write about these pressures, but this was written down. When I put the question to you before, I didn't know that this document existed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to read this first, please. It says: "I should like to mention that while being detained," these four men, "and the taking of official notes by our department," which means the process where our department staff take official notes from those four men, at that moment, we even had attempts of certain military policemen, their military policemen, their colleagues, trying physically to enter, even relatives, with the aim of preventing the act, itself; that is to say, that the members of our department should take these official notes, should be allowed to take these official notes down, and compile the minutes as a component part of a criminal report. So I think that is clear if you read it carefully, although I don't know what the interpretation you received was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, the English translation does not quite say what is said in your language. Members of your department, when one says "our department," one has the feeling that this relates to superiors. This is something you have specified. Good. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P06844. This is November --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm hearing the French.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a report from November 24th, and this regards those individuals. And under item -- or right before the end, it's a box. You can see that it's boxed out in the English. In regard to those individuals, it says: "After this, the suspects were kept in the Heliodrom because of disciplinary measures." Excuse me. If we can back up to the paragraph before, under item 3: "Examination of the said documentation of Heliodrom established that Busic, Coric, Pazin and Djenovic [phoen] were imprisoned in Heliodrom on July 16th for committing rape." And these are those individuals we've just been speaking about. "And on July 19th," three days later, "acting on a proposal from the regional military prosecutor in Mostar," and they mention the judge, "informed the Heliodrom that there were no longer legal conditions for continuing to hold the accused in detention and that they were to be set free. "After this, the suspects were kept in the Heliodrom because of disciplinary measures ordered by their commander, lasting 30 days. It can be seen from the duty diary that the accused were released from prison on 15 and 16 August 1993 after serving their sentence." Mr. Vidovic, perhaps you've had a little time to think about this, but these men were never convicted and sentenced for their crime, were they? The extent of their detention was three days plus 30 for disciplinary measures. They were never convicted, were they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears correct, if we look at this document. This was a report which was made at a time when I was no longer a member of the military police, that is, the Military Police Centre of Mostar, and you can see on the last page the name of Mr. Ivan Vuksic. He is the man who succeeded me in the position of chief of Crime Department of the Military Police. But to get back to your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment before you supplement this. Since I have the document before me, it seems that these four individuals were under arrest, but Judge Bevanda, Drago Bevanda, released them, feeling that they no longer met the legal conditions to be detained. So they were released. They will serve their disciplinary sentence. So what I don't know, on the basis of this document, is this: The investigating judge releases them, but was the Tribunal seized of this or not? Because as I understand your procedure, the investigating judge must send the case to the prosecutor, who must then seize the Tribunal. Perhaps the prosecutor in Mostar didn't do anything about this. Did you have any information to that effect or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot say what happened in this case. I did the work from my remit, and I submitted -- or, rather, forwarded the file on, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for having interrupted you, because you wanted to add something to this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to add, what have I just told you and the Prosecutor, I'm glad that you asked the question to me again, because this is an obvious example of the fact that the service where I worked and whose head I was for a time was not prevented from filing a criminal report, but the conditions under which we worked, and what happened subsequently, is outside of the scope of my jurisdiction. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a minute. I only want to say -- could Mr. Kovacic please switch off his microphone. I just want to say that the Coric Defence presented evidence from the court register of the Military Court in Mostar showing that these persons were convicted. I don't have the transcript here, but I can promise the Bench that by tomorrow I'll submit it. We have documents, from the criminal report to the verdict of the Military Court in Mostar. I'm positive about this case. By tomorrow, I can show you the page of the transcript where this was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, according to the Defence lawyer, we know that at the end of the day they were convicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The Prosecution's position is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's wait for tomorrow for the suspense.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, when you were speaking about these crimes, you also spoke about 5D04181, and this was a document regarding a theft that the military police had investigated, a theft from a detainee at Dretelj. Do you remember speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this criminal report? Is it the one I see here before me?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, no. Your testimony the other day, you spoke about a number of criminal reports. One of them regarded a theft by an HVO soldier at Dretelj. Do you remember talking about that? You have to say, Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember which report exactly. But if we spoke about criminal reports for theft, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, the Trial Chamber will remember your testimony about this. At this point, I'd like to show you a video, a video that was internationally aired at the end of August, beginning of September of 1993. It's P00977, and it's in French. The English translation is in the first part of the binder. It's 977. There will be B/C/S subtitles.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm also going to show you P04588 that will appear on the screen in a moment. This is also a picture of one of the prisoners at Dretelj. Mr. Vidovic, you have shared with us an investigation into a crime at Dretelj, and that was the theft of money from a detainee. So in sharing that particular report with this Trial Chamber, are you telling the Trial Chamber that that was the extent of the HVO military police investigations at Dretelj at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't work at Dretelj. I worked in Mostar. I doubt that I conducted the investigation you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the reason I mention it is because it's one of the investigations you spoke about on Monday. But I'll ask you a separate question. The video that we just played was something that was aired internationally. I think it was August 31st. It was aired all over Bosnia-Herzegovina and was well known. At the time, didn't you see these images or hear about what was going on at Dretelj, and think that the military police better get down there and investigate, or did you think that the military police was not doing that because they didn't think the maltreatment at Dretelj was a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can reply in only one way. At that time, I worked for the Crime Department of the Mostar Centre. I've never been at Dretelj, nor was it within my territorial jurisdiction. I worked for the Crime Department of the Mostar Centre, first in the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police and later in the 5th Battalion, as I said two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But if you had seen these images in August and early September of 1993 and you were in the zone that had Dretelj in it, wouldn't you agree with me that, as a military police officer, you'd think you better go to Dretelj and investigate?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I couldn't go to Dretelj. That wasn't my area of responsibility. I was at the Crime Centre of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And right now I'm only asking you in a general way, based on your experience as a military police investigator. If you had seen something like this and Dretelj was within your zone, after seeing this, don't you think you would have gone down to investigate?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give you a general answer. Well, in principle, I would have done that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of any HVO military police investigations and prosecutions regarding the maltreatment of the prisoners at Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to move on, and this is the same binder. It's part 3. And first let me just ask you a couple of questions before you get there. You had indicated, in your direct testimony, that you didn't investigate using any bias. And, for example, I think you told me earlier today that you didn't -- you never not investigated because the victims of the crime were Muslims, for example. Did you ever not investigate a crime because the perpetrators were people that the HVO wanted to protect?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have repeated a zillion times here that we launched investigations once we received information about a crime. I couldn't have knowledge of all crimes committed in a town like Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to go to P03928, 3928. And this is a special report to Valentin Coric, and it's compiled by Officer Toni Ramljak. Toni Ramljak is somebody earlier today you mentioned who worked with you; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is August 3rd, and it says: "The staff of this department have noticed lately that members of the so-called ATG units are responsible for a large share of the crime in the Mostar town area and that the Vinko Skrobo ATG and the Benko Penavic ATG are the most prominent among them, and since these two units are listed as parts of the Convicts Battalion, they have special status for unknown reasons. This special status is reflected in the fact that neither the military police, nor any other law enforcement organ, is taking any measures against the members of these units who commit crimes. As far as the Department of Military Crime Police Centre Mostar is concerned, centre head Zvonko Vidovic received an order some time ago from the chief of the Military Police Administration that the centre should only register certain acts committed by certain people from these units ..." Mr. Vidovic, do you remember receiving an order from Mr. Coric in regard to not investigating these ATGs?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we remember what I spoke about a short while ago about those meetings with the MUP, which they hosted, and then with the military police five days later, which we hosted, somewhere in between those occasions I received an instruction from Chief Coric saying that all criminal offences linked to these two units and their soldiers should be -- we should collect information on all them, we should register them all, and that it will be used in a comprehensive operation, the purpose of which will be bringing the perpetrators to justice. Because if we follow the sequence of documents carefully, then we will see that they keep reappearing as perpetrators of serious crimes. And I believe that operation was, indeed, later launched in co-operation with the MUP, the Military Prosecutor's Office, and the Military Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Vidovic. I understand you -- you say that Mr. Coric says, Collect all the information, register all the information, but at some point we're going to put it together in a big investigation and do it all at once; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. We had already sent a large number of documents, and then we continued collecting everything else that would be used for that large-scale operation. And if I may add, it was an operation which also involved military units because of -- because these groups were as dangerous as they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vidovic. But let's look again at this language, because I would submit that this language does not support what you've just said. It says: "... Vidovic received an order some time ago from Coric that the centre should only register certain acts committed by certain people from these units ..." Sir, I would submit to you that what this means is that every time somebody in one of the Convicts Battalion commits a crime, you should look the other way, and that sometimes you should register some of the acts with some of the people, but don't register them all. Sir, wouldn't you agree with me that that's what it says? It says ignore some of the crimes that they're committing, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This language is starting with certain people. Well, I cannot say that all members of those units were criminals automatically, but it was always the same people, specific people from those units, who kept committing crimes. We had notes of that, we had registered that, and we were preparing a larger-scale operation which would result in their arrest and the filing of a large number of criminal reports. At that time in Mostar, we had serious problems with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You did, sir. And let's go on to the next paragraph to talk about this a little bit more. Ramljak writes: "I would like to point out that of the entire personnel of the above-mentioned units," the Convicts Battalion, "a large part is involved in criminal activity, so that a vigorous pursuit action and the bringing of the perpetrators of criminal acts to court would probably lead to a break-up of those units." Mr. Vidovic, isn't it true that Mr. Coric was telling you to not investigate those units, because if you did, and if they were prosecuted and they were made to leave those units, that those units would ultimately break up; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contrary is true, the opposite. In various investigations, we were preparing to reach our ultimate goal. Mr. Coric, Mr. Ramljak, and I, as well as all staff of my unit, were involved in a broad operation which was meant to result in arrests. And the seven or eight of us from our department were unarmed, except for our pistols, and we worked in offices all the time. We were in no position to arrest those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let me put the Prosecution case to you, and then I'm going to ask a question and ask your comment. The Trial Chamber has heard time and time again that the Convicts Battalion was committing crime in Mostar, and, furthermore, they've heard that the Convicts Battalion didn't come under the normal chain of command of the HVO and instead reported directly to Boban. Yet, nonetheless, during this cross-examination we have seen a document in which you have complained to Stojic about the actions of the Convicts Battalion. You have complained to other HVO commanders about the actions of the Convicts Battalion, suggesting that at least from your perspective, you thought they came under the HVO. And it appears now, to keep them under control, that Mr. Coric is telling the Military Police Crime Investigative Services to not investigate them, and, Don't investigate all of them, because if you do, it's going to break up the units. Sir, wouldn't you agree that the real story is the Convicts Battalion was committing crimes, it was under the control of the HVO chain of command, but the HVO purposely did nothing about it, because if they had, it would have broken up one of their most effective and aggressive units? Isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you for two reasons. Firstly, now that you've put to me what I wrote to Mr. Stojic, well, that doesn't mean that Mr. Stojic was accountable for that. He was in no position to give orders to anyone, least of all to the Convicts Battalion. And, secondly, we are preparing a large-scale operation which, in the military police and in a war, can only be done in that way. So there must be comprehensive preparation, and there must be -- or we must request the support of military units to arrest such dangerous individuals, because you must know that these two units not only engage in criminal activities toward third persons; toward the end of summer of 1993, they also had a clash with each other, namely, the Vinko Skrobo and the Benko Penavic units, and there were some people wounded as a result, and we investigated that. I remember that Mr. Ramljak and I went to Split to interview the wounded to learn about the facts of that armed conflict in a rather peaceful part of town on the road from Mostar to Siroki Brijeg. So if you can follow what I'm saying, those were very dangerous units at the time, and I cannot say who was their direct superior at the time. If they were part of the Convicts Battalion, then it would probably have been the commander of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I inquire how much time I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for now, you have one minute left. Registrar, how much time does Ms. West have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have used two hours and forty-two minutes, which means that you have eighteen minutes left. So if you agree, we will carry on tomorrow for 18 minutes, and then there will be a redirect. Witness, you will have to come back tomorrow. Tomorrow, we will be sitting in the afternoon. So we will start at a quarter past 2.00, we'll have a break, and we will finish by 6.00 p.m., but I'm sure we'll have plenty of time. So we'll meet again tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of April, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
